slides.title: Freeze your credit. It's free.
slides.sub: It stops anyone, even you, from opening new credit in your name.

slides.heading: What a freeze does
body: While a credit freeze is on, nobody can open a new credit account in your name, including you. It's free to place and lift, and it doesn't hurt your credit score.
Why bother? Americans reported losing a record $15.9 billion to fraud in 2025.
slides.source: FTC Consumer Advice; FTC testimony, March 2026

slides.heading: How to do it
body: Contact all three credit bureaus: Equifax, Experian and TransUnion. Each one handles its own freeze.
Keep track of the account you set up with each bureau. You'll need it to lift the freeze later.
slides.source: FTC, Credit freezes and fraud alerts

slides.heading: Need credit? Lift it
body: Applying for a card, loan or apartment? Lift the freeze only at the bureau that lender uses, then put it back.
Under 16? A parent can request a free freeze for you too.

slides.takeaway: Freeze at all three bureaus. Lift it when you need credit.

posts.caption:
Americans reported losing a record $15.9 billion to fraud in 2025, across 3 million reports (FTC). One free move stops someone from opening credit in your name: a credit freeze.

While a freeze is on, nobody can open a new credit account in your name, including you. It's free to place and lift, and it doesn't affect your credit score. To set it up, contact all three bureaus: Equifax, Experian and TransUnion.

Need a card, loan or apartment later? Lift the freeze at the bureau that lender uses, then put it back. Parents can request a free freeze for kids under 16 too.

Data: FTC testimony to Congress (March 25, 2026); FTC Consumer Advice on credit freezes.
